newsitem.title: GREECE: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- MAY 13.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - GREEK GENERAL NEWS- MAY 13.

text.p: Leading stories in the Greek general press:

--Just as Athens denied that it had agreed to create air corridors in the Aergean for Turkish aircraft to use freely, Washington appears to be moving from pressure to threats to both countries with reports that the Clinton administration is imposing an informal embargo on armaments to the NATO allies. A senior State Department official is reported to have said that the sale of more arms to Athens and Ankara is pointless as long as the tension in the Aegean continues.

--Social dialogue on changes to the job market due to begin officially tomorrow between government, employers and unionists appears to be unravelling even before it starts. Unionists are chronically divided into party lines and were unable yesterday to agree on even one joint position to take into the talks.

--The 12th and final volume of the archives of former president of the republic and statesman Constantine Karamanlis is awaited with baited breath: the specific volume is expected to set off a new round of charges and counter-charges involving the major figures of the last 20 years - the late PASOK founder and president Andreas Papandreou and former New Democracy leader Constantine Mitsotakis.
--Taxi-driver Dimitris Vakrinos, self-confessed murderer of five people, took his own life yesterday while being held pending trial in an Athens jail.

--The Greek flag flew in the Former Yugoslav Republic of Macedonia yesterday where Greek troops have arrived for a nine-nation military exercise. However, FYROM President Kiro Gligorov is adamant that his country will not change its constitutional name - Athens, on the other hand, reiterated yesterday that it refuses to accept the country as "Macedonia".

--References in the Karamanlis archives have caused waves in the conservative opposition New Democracy with reports saying that former president Karamanlis planned to revise the references to Papandreou and Mitsotakis but was pipped at the post by leaks to the press.

--On May 29, the European Court of Justice will examine the Commission's suit against Greece on the excessive charges on imported secondhand cars. The Commission is expected to win the suit given that it is a clear case of violation of Community law and Greece's only argument is one of fears of environmental pollution.
--The American daughter-in-law of former king Constantine says she hopes Greece gets the 2004 Olympics and that she plans to attend them with her husband, Paul, Constantine's first-born.

--The fate of the enormous fortune of late shipping magnate Stavros Niarchos will be decided in the Swiss courts as Elena Ford, Niarchos's daughter by Charlotte Ford, has successfully filed an injunction after being left nothing by her father.
--Large tracts of land will be included in the country's town planning grid within the year, allowing the construction of more residential buildings.
